caption: Chiaverini v. City of Napoleon
proposition: Probable cause supporting ONE charge does not categorically defeat a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution claim (42 U.S.C. 1983) attacking a DIFFERENT charge in the same proceeding; the Sixth Circuit 'any-crime rule' is rejected. Kagan, J., 6-3. Probable cause must be assessed charge-by-charge where a baseless charge caused the seizure.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Chiaverini 2024 any-crime rule'; supremecourt.gov 23-50 slip op; CRS/Constitution Annotated; SCOTUSblog

caption: United States v. Felton
proposition: A warrant affidavit resting almost entirely on an uncorroborated confidential source, with material omissions about the informant's credibility, cannot support probable cause; Leon good faith cannot be applied BEFORE resolving a credible Franks challenge; a substantial preliminary showing of reckless/intentional omission entitles defendant to a Franks hearing. Denial of suppression reversed and remanded.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Felton 7th Cir 2025 Franks informant'; CA7 media opinion 23-1352; Justia; FindLaw; CaseMine

caption: Franks v. Delaware material-omission extension (unresolved split)
proposition: Whether and how Franks extends to reckless/intentional MATERIAL OMISSIONS (as opposed to affirmative falsehoods) remains unsettled: a majority of circuits (incl. 7th, 9th, 10th) apply Franks to omissions but SCOTUS has never approved that extension. A rigorous wiki should flag this as a live doctrine gap, reinforced by Felton (7th Cir. 2025).
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Franks materiality circuit split omissions'; W&M Bill of Rights J.; Felton commentary

caption: United States v. Johnson
proposition: A trained narcotics dog's sniff at the front door of an apartment located in a COMMON HALLWAY is not a Fourth Amendment search; the apartment threshold in a shared corridor is not constitutionally protected curtilage of the resident, distinguishing Florida v. Jardines (front porch of a single-family home). Deepens the multi-family-dwelling common-area split.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'K9 sniff apartment door common hallway 4th Cir 2025'; Harvard L. Rev. vol 139 note; NC Crim Law blog; Drugbeat

caption: United States v. Parkerson
proposition: A trespasser occupying a tent on POSTED public land has no objectively reasonable expectation of privacy (Katz objective prong fails), so a warrantless search of the tent does not implicate the Fourth Amendment. Sharpens a circuit split: 9th Cir. treats a tent as a protected dwelling regardless of authorization; 1st/5th/10th apply a trespass-defeats-privacy rule.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'homeless encampment tent Fourth Amendment 2025 circuit'; CaseMine commentary (Parkerson, 5th Cir. 2025)

caption: United States v. McGhee
proposition: Observations of a side yard/deck (blood spatter, powdery substance) made from the front yard (an open field) through an open side-yard fence are lawful plain-view observations from a lawful vantage; combined with exigency, warrantless entry and the ensuing warrant upheld. Guidance on the plain-view/curtilage/open-field boundary.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'plain view curtilage open field 2025 circuit'; DLG Learning Center analysis (McGhee, 8th Cir.)

caption: United States v. Rahmings
proposition: A defendant who discarded a backpack while fleeing police into a residence abandoned any reasonable expectation of privacy in its contents; the warrantless search of the abandoned effects did not violate the Fourth Amendment. Reaffirms abandonment/REP-forfeiture doctrine.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'abandonment Fourth Amendment 2024 2025 circuit'; LLRMI legal update (Rahmings, 11th Cir.)

caption: United States v. Burnett
proposition: Reaffirms the abandonment doctrine: no reasonable expectation of privacy in property voluntarily abandoned; warrantless search/seizure of abandoned property permissible. Companion contemporary application to Rahmings (11th Cir. 2024).
discovery_path: WebSearch 'abandonment Fourth Amendment 2025 circuit'; CaseMine commentary (Burnett v. USA, 7th Cir.)

caption: United States v. Banks
proposition: The front porch of a residence is curtilage entitled to the same Fourth Amendment protection as the home's interior; officers who avoided the normal front approach, cut through the backyard to surprise a felon on his porch, and seized him without a warrant violated the Fourth Amendment and tainted the evidence. Pre-2024 but treated as doctrine-shaping curtilage/knock-and-talk authority in 2024 commentary.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'front porch curtilage 2024 circuit'; LLRMI 2024 update; Lawstache (Feb 2024); CA7 22-1312

caption: Long Lake Township v. Maxon
court: Michigan Supreme Court (state) / Mich. Ct. App.
proposition: Leading vehicle on warrantless targeted DRONE surveillance: Mich. Ct. App. (2021) held low-altitude, targeted drone surveillance of a home/curtilage is a Fourth Amendment search (analogizing Kyllo); Mich. S. Ct. (2025) resolved on exclusionary-rule grounds without reaching the search question. Flags the unresolved federal aerial-surveillance/drone gap left after Ciraolo/Dow/Florida v. Riley. STATE court -- flagged as doctrine gap, not federal holding.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'drone surveillance Fourth Amendment 2024 2025 Long Lake Maxon'; Harvard L. Rev. vol 138; Lexology; Cato

caption: Open-fields doctrine reexamination (Hester/Oliver)
proposition: On the open-fields doctrine's 2024 centennial, sustained scholarly/litigation pressure (Institute for Justice 4th Amendment Project; George Mason L. Rev. Dec. 2024; Cato Spring 2024) and a wave of STATE high courts rejecting open fields under state constitutions frame Hester/Oliver as ripe for reexamination. A rigorous wiki should carry this as an active doctrine-ferment node.

caption: Mumford v. Iowa (cert denied) -- dog-intrusion-into-vehicle split
court: Iowa S. Ct. / U.S. Supreme Court (cert denied)
proposition: Cert denied over a documented circuit split on whether a drug dog's brief physical intrusion into a vehicle's interior (nose/paws through an open window) is a trespassory Fourth Amendment search: 5th and 9th Cir. treat an officer's or dog's breach of the interior as a trespass/search; Iowa S. Ct. (and others) do not. Marks a live canine-as-search split SCOTUS declined to resolve.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Mumford v Iowa dog sniff car interior cert 2025'; SCOTUSblog case file; cert pet. 24-1093

caption: Barnes v. Felix
proposition: Fourth Amendment excessive-force reasonableness (Graham v. Connor) is judged on the TOTALITY OF THE CIRCUMSTANCES, including the events leading up to the use of force; the 'moment-of-the-threat' rule that confines the inquiry to the precise instant of danger (5th Cir. and others) is rejected. Unanimous (Kagan, J.); Kavanaugh concurrence on traffic-stop dangers.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Barnes v Felix 2025 moment of threat'; supremecourt.gov 23-1239 slip op; CRS LSB11336; Harvard L. Rev. vol 139

caption: United States v. Wilson
proposition: Post-NYSRPA v. Bruen, suspected mere possession of a concealed firearm -- presumptively lawful under state (Louisiana) law -- cannot by itself supply reasonable suspicion for a Terry stop (though the seizure was sustained on other facts). Illustrates a growing post-Bruen split/tension (2d Cir. voicing parallel doubts) over whether gun possession alone justifies an investigative stop.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Terry stop gun high crime 2024 2025 circuit Bruen'; Stanford L. Rev. Online 'Emerging Firearms Hypocrisy of Terry'

caption: Prolonged-seizure / 'time as a constitutional constraint' split (Rodriguez progeny)
proposition: Circuits remain split on how long a Fourth Amendment seizure (traffic stop/detention) may last before it becomes unreasonable and on how to measure mission-related delay versus unrelated extension under Rodriguez v. United States. Recent commentary (Washington Law Review) frames this as an unresolved split ripe for review. Flagged as a doctrine node absent a single new controlling caption.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Fourth Amendment circuit split 2025 2026 seizure'; Washington Law Review 'Time as a Constitutional Constraint'

caption: United States v. Chatrie
court: U.S. Supreme Court (below: 4th Cir. en banc)
cite_or_docket: 609 U.S. ___ (2026); No. 25-112; 4th Cir. en banc per curiam (14-1)
proposition: Government conducts a Fourth Amendment SEARCH when it accesses geofence location data a user provides to a provider; remanded to decide whether the multi-step geofence warrant satisfied probable cause and PARTICULARITY (general-warrant concern). 4th Cir. en banc had affirmed no-suppression per curiam (14-1, 8 concurrences, 1 dissent). NOTE: geofence overlaps the digital-surveillance umbrella -- dedupe against S6 digital saturation logs; included here for the warrant-particularity/general-warrant doctrine grain.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'geofence warrant particularity Chatrie en banc'; supremecourt.gov 25-112; CRS LSB11274; Brookings; Justia 609 U.S.

caption: United States v. Smith
proposition: Geofence warrants are 'modern-day general warrants' that violate the Fourth Amendment because they lack particularity -- they compel disclosure of all devices within a broad area with no individualized suspicion -- though suppression was denied under Leon good faith. Splits with the 4th Cir. Chatrie approach; a core particularity/general-warrant holding. NOTE: digital-overlap -- dedupe against S6 digital logs.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'geofence warrant Smith Fifth Circuit general warrant 2024'; Brookings; CDT; CRS LSB11274

caption: United States v. Williams
proposition: Reaffirms (per Hudson v. Michigan) that SUPPRESSION is not an available remedy for a knock-and-announce violation during warrant execution; and recognizes exigency exceptions -- threat of physical violence, likely destruction of evidence, or futility -- excusing the knock-and-announce requirement under the Fourth Amendment and 18 U.S.C. 3109.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'knock and announce 2024 2025 circuit execution warrant'; NC Crim Law 4th Cir March 2025 summaries; 130 F.4th 177

caption: Case v. Montana
proposition: Under the EMERGENCY-AID exception, police may make a warrantless entry into a home when they have 'an objectively reasonable basis for believing' an occupant is seriously injured or imminently threatened with serious harm; PROBABLE CAUSE is NOT required (probable cause is a criminal/investigative concept, not a public-safety one), and the standard is distinct from reasonable suspicion's specific-and-articulable-facts test. Clarifies Brigham City v. Stuart / post-Caniglia emergency-aid doctrine. Unanimous.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'Case v Montana emergency aid probable cause 2026'; supremecourt.gov 24-624 slip op; CRS LSB11394; ABA Preview; SCOTUSblog

caption: United States v. Davis
proposition: Upholds a warrantless vehicle search under BOTH the search-incident-to-arrest exception (Arizona v. Gant's 'reason to believe evidence of the offense of arrest might be found' prong, which requires only a reasonable basis, not probable cause) and the automobile exception; declines to collapse Gant's evidentiary-belief prong into the automobile exception's probable-cause standard.
discovery_path: WebSearch 'search incident automobile exception Gant 2024 circuit'; DLG Learning Center (Davis, 7th Cir.); Justia 23-2259; 119 F.4th 500
